newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germans march nationwide to protest austerity plan.
newsitem.headline: Germans march nationwide to protest austerity plan.

text.p: More than 200,000 trade union workers marched through six of Germany's largest cities on Saturday to protest against the government's plans to trim the country's generous welfare spending.
Union leaders blasted Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government, telling workers at rallies in Berlin, Hamburg, Stuttgart, Dortmund, Leipzig and Ludwigshafen that the austerity package was unfair.

"The German constitution does not guarantee free market domination or the right to maximise profits or the exploitation of workers," said Ursula Engelen-Kefer, deputy chairman of the German Trade Union Federation (DGB) at the rally in Berlin.

"The unholy alliance of government and employers has come up with this savings plan that will divide our society," she told 50,000 people in front of the Brandenburg Gate. "We will take our fight against this plan further."

The protests, the sequel to a July demonstration in Bonn that brought 350,000 into the city centre, came just days before the Bundestag, or lower house, is scheduled to vote on the government's austerity measures.
Union leaders said 240,000 took part in the six rallies nationwide on Saturday.

The government has said it needs to cut public spending by 50 billion marks ($33 billion) and social security spending by 20 billion marks in 1997 in a bid to reduce its budget deficit enough to ensure Germany qualifies for the single European currency.

Designed to reduce the country's 10 percent unemployment rate and stop companies from exporting thousands of jobs abroad each year to escape the high labour costs, Kohl's austerity package would trim pensions, sick pay and other benefits.

Germany has the most comprehensive social net in the world, industry leaders say, devoting one third of its total economic output on social spending. Workers have six weeks' paid holiday and call in sick on average another four weeks each year.

"A nation has no future when those who do their duty are considered dumb," Kohl said in a speech on Friday night in Hanover. "The almighty God for Germans cannot be leisure time. We are talking about the future, not about leisure time."

Carrying banners reading "There is enough money" and "Stop the social destruction plan", workers and family members from dozens of separate trade unions marched peacefully through the various city centres under mostly sunny late summer skies.
Leading members of the opposition Social Democratic Party (SPD), which has tried to block the austerity plan in parliament, attended the rallies as well to lend moral support. ($1=1.4854 Mark)
